children.text: A mountain in Itogon about
1 hour
by car from Baguio, standing at about
, with a traverse trail of about
9.4km
through pine forest and grassy ridges. Thanks to the cliff-edge Gungal Rock and views of the Cordillera mountain ranges, it's a beloved day hike that even beginners can take on.
Mount Ulap rises to about

in Itogon, south of Baguio, between the villages of Ampucao and Santa Fe. "Ulap" means "cloud" in Filipino, and true to its name, early mornings often bring clouds blanketing the valleys below and mist drifting along the ridges. Since Barangay Ampucao officially opened it as an ecotourism trail (the Mt. Ulap Eco-Trail) in
, it has quickly become one of the Philippines' signature day hikes.
The route is a traverse trail of about
9.4km

, starting at Ampucao Barangay Hall, crossing several peaks, and descending to Santa Fe. Benguet pine forest, open grassy ridges, and rocky peaks alternate along the way, and on clear days you can see as far as Mount Pulag and the Cordillera ranges, and even the lowland plains toward Lingayen Gulf to the west. The steep sections aren't long, so with reasonable fitness even hiking beginners can complete it.

Itogon, where the mountain stands, covers about 450km² and is the largest municipality in Benguet. It is also a gold-mining area where the Philippines' first large-scale mining began with the founding of Benguet Corporation in

. About 60% of residents are Ibaloi and about 40% are Kankanaey, and the area around Mount Ulap lies within the Ibaloi ancestral domain. Before the trail opened, it was also used as part of the course for The North Face 100 trail running race.

Mount Ulap became especially famous thanks to "Gungal Rock." Photos taken standing on the tip of this rock, which juts out into thin air from the ridge, have been shared countless times on Philippine social media, and many hikers still queue up in front of it today. Because traditional Ibaloi burial caves and sacred sites lie along the trail, the local community manages the trail directly.

Mount Ulap suits travelers who want an easy mountain outing from Baguio without Pulag's predawn cold or complicated reservations, as well as those who want to warm up before starting a Cordillera mountain trip.
A one-way route of about
9.4km
, taking
5–7 hours
including rest stops. Its advantage is that you never retrace your steps, so the scenery keeps changing.

The signature spot midway along the ridge, where you take photos standing on a rock jutting out over the cliff. Follow your guide's instructions and wait your turn, and as a rule, don't stand at the very edge on windy days.

blocks.title: First views from Ambanaw Pa-oay Peak

children.text: At
, this is the first peak you reach, about
3.6km
from the trailhead after a climb through the pine forest. Arrive early in the morning to see sunlight spilling over the clouds that fill the valleys.

blocks.title: A Cordillera panorama from the Ulap summit

children.text: From the summit at about
, layered mountain ranges and mining areas spread out below, and on a clear day even the lowland plains come into view.

Most of the route runs through Benguet pine forest and grassland, so the sound of the wind and the scent of pine leave a strong impression. This is a mountain where the walk itself is more memorable than the photos.

Because most guides are local residents, they share stories about the burial caves, ancestor-worship traditions, and the history of the mining villages. Asking them questions makes the hike much richer.

blocks.title: Two-day trip with a night in Baguio

children.text: Stay in Baguio the night before and set off at dawn, and you can finish the trail with time to spare, then relax and eat in downtown Baguio in the afternoon.

blocks.title: Pong-ol burial cave and hanging bridges

children.text: The descent from the summit to the Santa Fe exit passes the Pong-ol burial cave, which holds the remains of Ibaloi ancestors, and several steel hanging bridges. The cave is a sacred site, so the rule is not to touch or photograph it, and the hanging bridges sway, so hold the railing and cross slowly.

The steepest climb is the stretch from the trailhead at Ampucao Barangay Hall (about
above sea level) to the first peak, Ambanaw Pa-oay: about
3.6km
, taking
1–2 hours
. Past this peak the gradient eases, and from there the trail rises and falls repeatedly along the ridge.
The total elevation gain is about
, so if you can normally walk a local hill for
3–4 hours
, you have enough stamina. However, the descent of about
from the summit to the Santa Fe exit (about
above sea level) is steep and slippery with dirt and pine needles, so slow down.
Key points along the way are Ambanaw Pa-oay Peak (
) at about
3.6km
from the trailhead, Gungal Rock (
) at about
5.4km
, and the Ulap summit (
) at about
6.5km
; after that, the trail passes the Pong-ol burial cave and the hanging bridges before reaching the Santa Fe exit at the
9.4km
mark. The Philippine hiking site Pinoy Mountaineer rates its difficulty 3 out of 9.
Leave Baguio, register for camping at Ampucao Barangay Hall, and get assigned a camping guide (about
per group)
Pass Ambanaw Pa-oay Peak and Gungal Rock, then pitch your tent at the campsite near the summit
Watch the sunset from the ridge; temperatures drop sharply at night, so bring warm clothes and a sleeping bag
Watch the sunrise and the sea of clouds filling the valleys from near the summit
Descend past the Pong-ol burial cave and the hanging bridges to the Santa Fe exit, then return to Baguio by jeepney
Camping registration closes at
, and a campsite fee is charged separately from the guide fee. Whether camping is allowed and how much it costs can change depending on the season, so check the official page before you go.
Take a Baguio-bound bus (Victory Liner, JoyBus, Solid North, etc.) from Cubao, Pasay, and elsewhere, taking about
4–6 hours
and costing about
. For a dawn hike, arriving in Baguio the day before and staying one night is recommended.

Victory Liner departs from Cubao and Pasay, Genesis and JoyBus from Cubao, Pasay, and Avenida, and Solid North from its PITX and Cubao terminals, with buses running almost 24 hours a day. If you can't stay in Baguio the night before, another option is to take a night bus leaving around
10:00 PM–midnight
, arrive in Baguio at dawn, and go straight to Ampucao by taxi.
Genesis buses run several times a day from Clark International Airport (CRK) to Baguio, taking about
3–4 hours
and costing about
. The arrival terminal in Baguio is on Gov. Pack Road. If your flight lands late at night, spend a night in Baguio and set out on the hike at dawn the next day.
It takes about
4–5 hours
from Manila to Baguio via NLEX–SCTEX–TPLEX, and about
30–45 minutes
from Baguio to Ampucao. Enter "Ampucao Elementary School" as your navigation destination to be guided to the area near the registration point; parking costs about
per vehicle.
Because this is a traverse, your car stays at the trailhead while you descend to Santa Fe, so the driver has to take a taxi or van from the exit back to Ampucao to retrieve it.
From the jeepney stop for Philex Mine in downtown Baguio, take a jeepney bound for Philex and get off at "Ampucao Barangay Hall." It takes about
40 minutes–1 hour
, for a fare of about
per person. The first jeepney of the day may not depart very early, so check at the stop the day before.
If you're traveling with others, a taxi or chartered van is more convenient. By taxi it takes about
30–45 minutes
, and it's best to negotiate a fare that includes waiting at the Santa Fe exit and driving you back.

The jeepney stop is on Lakandula Street (toward Magsaysay Avenue) next to Baguio Center Mall; tell the driver you're going to Mount Ulap and you'll be dropped off in front of Ampucao Barangay Hall. Registration opens at
on weekends and
on weekdays, and closes at
noon
for day hikes and
for camping, so arrive by late morning at the latest. You need an ID to register. Jeepneys between Ampucao and Baguio run until around
At the descent point on the Philex roadside in Santa Fe, you can catch a jeepney back to Baguio. Departures can space out in the afternoon, so try not to finish the descent too late.
From the exit to the main road, take a shared van or tricycle (about
per person), then transfer to a Baguio-bound jeepney, which takes about
1 hour
and costs about
. If you left your car in Ampucao, hire a taxi or van from the exit to Ampucao for about
per vehicle and go back to pick it up.
An overnight join tour departing from Manila (including round-trip van, registration fee, and guide) costs about
per person, and is convenient since you don't need to arrange transport yourself.
The dry season,
November–April
, is best.
December–February
in particular has cool dawn temperatures around
, giving a high chance of seeing a sea of clouds and making walking pleasant even during the day.
March–May
has many clear days and the widest visibility, but the ridge has little shade at midday and the sun is very strong, so an early start is essential.
During the rainy season,
June–October

, afternoon rain and thick fog make the views hard to see. The dirt trail becomes slippery, and the trail may close if a typhoon comes. On weekends and public holidays, hikers crowd in and you may have to wait a long time at Gungal Rock, so a weekday hike is recommended if possible.
According to Baguio weather records, January rainfall is only about 16mm, while August is the wettest month at about 963mm. In
February
, when Baguio's Panagbenga Flower Festival takes place, during Holy Week (
), and over the year-end holidays, Baguio accommodation and buses fill up early and the line at Gungal Rock grows longer, so book early. At the end of the dry season, in
March–April
, the high risk of forest fires means the trail sometimes closes without notice.

items.label: Accommodation in Baguio
items.note: Staying the night before is recommended

children.text: Prices are approximate as of
and may vary depending on local conditions.
There is almost no accommodation around Mount Ulap, so staying in downtown Baguio is the usual approach. Booking a guesthouse (about
per night) or mid-range hotel (about
or more) in the city center near the Philex jeepney stop, around Session Road and Burnham Park, makes for an easy dawn departure.
At the Ampucao starting point there are small stores selling water and snacks, and near the summit a simple eatery serves rice with one side dish for about

a meal. However, the menu is limited and prices are higher than in town, so stock up on a packed lunch, bread, fruit, and chocolate at a convenience store or market in Baguio the day before. Back in Baguio after the hike, bulalo (beef bone marrow soup), Benguet vegetable dishes, and strawberry taho make a great reward for tired legs.

The Santa Fe exit has restrooms, food stalls, souvenir shops, and paid showers, so you can wash off the sweat before heading back to Baguio. For souvenirs, the ube jam, strawberry jam, and peanut brittle sold at the Good Shepherd Convent on Gibraltar Road in Baguio are famous, and at the Baguio Public Market you can buy Benguet strawberries and highland vegetables.
A guide is mandatory. Registration is normally done on the spot at Ampucao Barangay Hall, but groups of 15 or more may need to book in advance, so contact them through the official page.
Bring at least 1.5–2 liters of water. Water is also sold at the simple stalls near the summit, but it costs much more than in town.
A hat, sunscreen, and sunglasses are essential. UV exposure is strong at this altitude, and long stretches of the trail have no shade.
Dawn is chilly, so bring a light windbreaker and pack it away once the sun rises.
For photos at Gungal Rock, arriving before
8–9 AM
means a shorter wait.
Wear trekking shoes or sneakers with good grip. The dirt trail and pine needles on the descent are slippery.
Phone signal is available on the peaks but weak in the valleys. Save your guide's and your group's contact numbers with each other.
Only cash is accepted, so bring small bills for the registration and guide fees.
Trekking poles greatly reduce the strain on your knees on the long descent toward Santa Fe.
If you're a beginner, taking a light walk around downtown Baguio the day before to adjust to the altitude (about
above sea level) makes the first climb noticeably easier.
Gungal Rock is a cliff edge with no safety railing. Don't stand at the edge when the wind is strong or the rock is wet, and follow your guide's instructions.
The dirt trail is very slippery after rain. Bring trekking poles during the rainy season and avoid pushing yourself too hard.
The burial caves and ritual sites around the trail are sacred places. Don't touch them or enter.
All trash must be carried back down, and smoking and lighting fires are prohibited.
The trail may be temporarily closed due to weather or local circumstances, so check the official page's latest notices before setting out.
Trekking is suspended entirely during forest fires at the end of the dry season or during typhoons and heavy rain. In
, too, hiking was banned from
April 20–May 1
due to forest fires, and from
August 5–September 16
due to Tropical Storm Maymay and the southwest monsoon (habagat).
Descending in the late afternoon is risky, since public transport can stop running. Plan to reach Santa Fe by no later than
2–3 PM

by car, good for accommodation, meals, and city sightseeing before or after the hike.
About
2–3 hours
by car from Baguio, Luzon's highest peak, a good next challenge after warming up on Ulap.
